The UAlbany release makes the methodological carry-over explicit: the C-TAP frame-differencing software is 'similar to an approach used by physicists like him and Levy to look for direct evidence of dark matter'. This is the mechanism by which rare-event detection practice reached UAP field work at this institution.

edges.note: The UAlbany News Center release of 4 June 2025 states: 'Utilizing a diverse set of devices to capture different types of data on many channels, UAlbany authors Matthew Szydagis, Kevin Knuth and Cecilia Levy, along with Ben Kugielsky of UAPx, a non-profit scientific research organization, collected observable-light and infrared images during a field expedition in 2021 to Laguna Beach, California.' The release also records the outcome honestly - 'the UAlbany research team succeeded in plausibly explaining all but one of the potential anomalies detected' - and quotes Szydagis on the single unresolved ambiguity. A state university issuing a press release claiming a UAP field-instrumentation result as institutional output is the substantive reason this node belongs on the board.

edges.label: Academic base of UAPx's science leadership - NOT a host, sponsor or funder
edges.note: The distinction matters and is drawn by the University itself. UAlbany's release separates 'UAlbany authors Matthew Szydagis, Kevin Knuth and Cecilia Levy' from 'Ben Kugielsky of UAPx, a non-profit scientific research organization'. UAPx is an independent 501(c)(3); the University is where its two lead scientists hold their chairs, not its institutional home. This is the opposite of the harvard-cfa / galileo-project relationship already on the board, where the CfA is the host institution. Funding for the 2021 California field work came from Caroline Cory of OMnium Media, to produce the documentary 'A Tear in the Sky' (2022) - not from UAlbany.
